name: Lucius Annaeus Seneca
credit: Bronze bust once called Seneca, now known as the “Pseudo-Seneca” (Herculaneum; National Archaeological Museum, Naples), photograph by Brogi, c. 1908 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca, known as Seneca the Younger, was born at Corduba (Córdoba) in Spain and brought up in Rome, where he became a leading Stoic philosopher, a senator and a writer of letters, essays and tragedies. He served as tutor and then adviser to the young Emperor Nero, and grew immensely wealthy in that office.

Ten tragedies on Greek mythological themes survive under his name, among them Medea, Phaedra and Thyestes. Written in Latin verse, they are rhetorical and violent, and they were a decisive influence on the revenge tragedy of the English Renaissance. In AD 65 Seneca was implicated in the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero and was ordered to take his own life.
This archive presents his Medea in Frank Justus Miller’s 1907 English verse translation, and will add his other tragedies in time.
